transcript:
Date/Time: 2026-12-29 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Ana (ClearWave CTO), Samir (ML Eng), Jo (Product), Ravi (Security)

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh — this is our weekly POC sync. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Ana: Ana here.
[00:09] Samir: Samir on the line.
[00:11] Jo: Jo here.
[00:13] Ravi: Ravi, security.
[00:15] Marcus: Marcus, Redwood SE.
[00:17] Lena: Cool. So agenda: we wanted to review the run results from last week, talk model selection and talk about pinning and fallback strategy, and then next steps. Marcus, do you want to kick off with the benchmark summary?
[00:30] Marcus: Yeah, sure. Uh, so we ran the customer prompt set — thanks Samir for sending — across three candidates: rdx-3.1-q4 (our larger quantized variant), rdx-3.0-int8 (older but cheaper int8 path), and rdx-2.7-ff (smaller, low-latency). The high level: rdx-3.1-q4 gives the best quality on the edge cases, but 95th percentile latency is about 420ms under your p99-ish concurrency pattern, cost is approximately 1.8x of the int8 path. rdx-3.0-int8 sits at ~280ms p95 and is about 1.0x cost baseline. rdx-2.7-ff is the fastest at 220ms p95 but fails on some long-context summarization cases.
[01:10] Samir: Quick Q — what was the sequence length distribution you used? Our traffic has a long tail up to 2.5k tokens.
[01:18] Marcus: Right, um we used the distribution you sent but bucketed: median ~120 tokens, p90 ~650, p95 ~1.3k, p99 ~2.1k — so that long tail is in there which is why rdx-2.7 trips on the long context.
[01:35] Jo: And quality — how did you measure the "fails" on the long context?
[01:38] Marcus: It was two things: first, hallucination rates on the reference eval were materially higher for the 2.7, and second, truncation/beam issues for very long sequences. We also ran a small human eval for 200 examples and saw an approx 7% drop in correctness on long-context retrieval tasks.
[01:55] Ana: Hmm okay. Our priority is correctness for clinical notes summarization — latency is important but not at the cost of wrong outputs.
[02:01] Lena: Totally, that's helpful context. So given that, what are you recommending for pinning?
[02:06] Marcus: My recommendation: pin primary to rdx-3.1-q4 for the pilot — it balances quality with reasonable latency. For cost control and graceful degradation, configure fallback to rdx-3.0-int8 when queuing or latency SLOs are threatened. Also, we suggest autoscale policies that allow short bursts on dedicated capacity or re-route to hosted region that is underutilized.
[02:30] Samir: If we pin to rdx-3.1-q4, what does rollback look like if we see a regression?
[02:35] Marcus: Good question. We have a rollback playbook: first, immediate pin swap to the previous stable (we keep pinned versions per route), then automated A/B replays on the last 10k requests against older model to confirm behavior. We also keep a shadow log of inputs+outputs for 30 days in the pilot so you can run quick diffs. The swap is fast, usually under 2 minutes for config propagation.
[02:57] Ravi: On the logging/shadowing — how's data encrypted and can we route logs to our S3 in our VPC?
[03:04] Marcus: Yes, for Private/Dedicated you can send logs to your endpoint, and we support customer-side KMS. Right now for the hosted pilot the logs are in Redwood storage with server-side encryption; we can enable envelope encryption with your KMS per the checklist.
[03:18] Ravi: Okay please add that to the checklist.
[03:21] Lena: Noted. Marcus, can you talk about fallback policy details — like when to trigger fallback vs when to queue?
[03:28] Marcus: Sure. Our recommendations: fallback triggers when estimated per-request latency exceeds your SLO for more than N consecutive requests (configurable, default 3). Otherwise, queue with a short wait (up to 250ms) if it's a transient burst. For stateful sessions (chat) we prefer fallback to be a compatible variant to avoid context drift — so rdx-3.0-int8 is compatible for you. For more aggressive cost saving, you can configure a staged fallback to rdx-2.7-ff for non-critical routes.
[04:00] Samir: How about tokenization differences between models — could that cause subtle diffs when falling back?
[04:05] Marcus: Good call. Tokenization is pretty consistent across the rdx family but there are small differences in quantization and prompt post-processing. We recommend including a small sanity check suite in your rollout to detect tokenization drift; Redwood's routing can run a quick canonicalizer step to normalize prompts.
[04:20] Jo: Can we pin by route? I want critical routes pinned to 3.1 and less critical to int8.
[04:25] Marcus: Yep, route-level pinning is supported — per-route config with inheritance and overrides. You can also define rollout percentages for canary style pinning (10/50/100).
[04:34] Ana: Timeframe — if we decide to pin, how long until we can go live with the pilot? We need legal + security signoff too.
[04:40] Lena: From Redwood side, once you approve pricing and pinning config we can enable the pinned routes in your sandbox within 48 hours. Security signoff timeline is dependent on your side — any blockers?
[04:50] Ravi: Mostly KMS and SAML metadata; we have a compliance review next week. Also need the SOC2 attestation and audit logs sample.
[04:58] Marcus: We'll share the SOC2 report and an audit log sample — I'll add to the drive after this call.
[05:03] Samir: One more — can we get exact cost delta numbers? The 1.8x is rough.
[05:07] Marcus: Yes, Lena will follow up with a line-item comparison. For roughs: rdx-3.1-q4 = $0.036 per 1k tokens in pilot pricing, rdx-3.0-int8 = $0.02 per 1k tokens, rdx-2.7-ff = $0.012 per 1k. Those are ballparks; I'll confirm with pricing.
[05:26] Lena: I'll share a pricing breakdown.
[05:29] Jo: Are there any other risks we should be aware of?
[05:32] Marcus: Model regression risk on new versions — which is why we suggest pinning and canary rollouts plus eval suites. Also, heavy long-context requests can increase KV cache pressure; we can tune the cache TTL and prefetch heuristics.
[05:45] Samir: For the benchmark you ran, did you use GPU instances with the same shape as our Dedicated estimate? Because we want numbers that mirror Dedicated.
[05:53] Marcus: We used GDX-16 single-GPU nodes, which closely match your proposed Dedicated. If you want, we can run the same benchmark on your exact Dedicated shape — that would be part of a pilot performance run.
[06:05] Ana: That would be helpful. Also would like a test where we push to our p95 concurrency to simulate peak day.
[06:12] Marcus: Yep we can do a stress run. Samir, please confirm target concurrency and we'll schedule.
[06:18] Samir: I'll send numbers after the call.
[06:21] Lena: Great. Any questions from the security side?
[06:23] Ravi: For the shadow logs, retention — can we shorten to 7 days for pilot?
[06:27] Marcus: Yes, retention is configurable per-customer.
[06:29] Ravi: And can we have an option to redact PHI from logs before storing?
[06:33] Marcus: We have a redaction pipeline we can configure; however, that adds processing latency, so it's a tradeoff. We'll include the expected latency delta in the doc.
[06:43] Lena: Ok, let's recap next steps. Marcus?
[06:46] Marcus: I'll run the extra 95th percentile benchmark on rdx-3.1-q4 vs rdx-3.0-int8 using the full prompt set Samir gives, and post results. I'll also upload SOC2 and audit log sample.
[06:57] Lena: I'll send pricing delta and the pinning config + rollback playbook.
[07:01] Samir: I'll share prompt set and concurrency numbers.
[07:04] Ravi: I'll confirm SAML metadata and KMS policy.
[07:07] Ana: We aim to decide by next Friday on pinning.
[07:10] Lena: Sounds good. We'll plan a follow-up performance review call next Tuesday — I'll send calendar invite.
[07:15] Jo: Thanks everyone.
[07:17] Lena: Thanks all — talk soon.
